2.text: The dart is used for ducks and geese, but it is too weak for the swan.

3.text: A kayaker, finding a moulting swan on a lake, usually tires

4.text: it by long pursuit, making it dive frequently. The swan is

5.text: not a good diver, and, because of its white plumage, can

6.text: generally be seen while swimming under water. Finally the

7.text: kayaker overtakes the swan when it comes to the surface. He

8.text: seizes it by its long neck, which he breaks close to the head.

9.text: Ptarmigans and ducks are also caught by means of a drop-

10.text: net fastened to a hoop. The birds are allured with bait strewn

11.text: on the ground, and at a favorable moment the net is lowered

12.text: by means of a long line.

13.text: FISHING. — Fishing is of comparatively less importance,
13.note: you SAID you did that and then didn't DO IT

14.text: because the coast of the Chukchee Peninsula is not very rich

15.text: in fish. On the Pacific coast the mouth of the Anadyr is the last

16.text: place to the north to which large shoals of Salmonidæ resort

17.text: every year to spawn. Farther on, their number rapidly diminishes.

18.text: On the Arctic shore, Coregonidæ begin to be abundant from Chaun

19.text: Bay, and especially from the mouth of the Kolyma westward.

20.text: Fish-nets of sinew are used everywhere by the Reindeer and Maritime

21.text: Chukchee. Their length varies greatly, according to whether they are employed

22.text: on the seashore, or in the rivers and lakes of the interior. The small net of

23.text: the Reindeer people, used in catching graylings, is made of from ten to fifteen

24.text: pieces of sinew. A larger net of the Pacific fishermen (Fig. 59) requires from

25.text: twenty to thirty pieces. The length of the latter varies from fifteen to twenty-

26.text: five feet; the meshes are from two to four inches square. Other nets are

27.text: made of thin strips of leather (Fig. 60), and in former times they were made

28.text: also of whalebone. The Reindeer people often make their nets without a

29.text: shuttle, though the process is very slow. The Maritime Chukchee use shuttles

30.text: of whalebone (Fig. 61, a), wood (Fig. 61, b, c), or bone, with netting-sticks
